issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: John, a 63-year-old married man of Oceania descent, works as a Financial Analyst in a bustling office. Despite his successful career and stable family life, he has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening car accident that occurred a year ago. The event left him with lingering fears and intrusive memories that disrupt his daily life. The night of the accident was particularly dark, and John vividly recalls the sharp smell of burning rubber and diesel as his vehicle careened off the road into a ditch. Since then, any whiff of petroleum or the sound of car horns sends him reeling back to that moment. The darkness of parking garages now triggers overwhelming anxiety, compelling him to avoid them entirely. His wife has noticed how he clings to her hand when they park at night, and even small sounds from passing cars can make his body react as if he were still in danger. John's body reacts before his mind comprehends the situation, leaving him feeling helpless and vulnerable. He wakes frequently during the night to check whether he is safe, scanning every shadow for potential threats. This hypervigilance has extended into his daily life; entering any room or building, John instinctively scans for exits as soon as he steps inside. The memory of that fateful night feels present rather than past, and auditory elements from the accident often replay in his mind—screeching brakes, shattering glass. These vivid recollections are triggered without warning by seemingly mundane events, such as a faint smell of gasoline or the sound of car doors slamming outside his office building. John’s hypervigilance is not just about being on guard; he believes that if he thinks too deeply about the event, he will not be able to handle it. This thought avoidance has created a paradoxical cycle where any trigger instantly brings back the full memory, further reinforcing his belief in constant vigilance. He feels he must remain especially careful because you never know what can happen next, which keeps him in a state of heightened alertness. The intrusive memories not only disrupt John’s present but also amplify his sense of threat. When he hears certain sounds or smells that remind him of the accident, his body immediately reacts as if danger is imminent, and he scans for exits to ensure there's an escape route if needed. This constant scanning has led to a rigid routine where he avoids dark places and any situation that might trigger a memory. John’s workplace is particularly challenging; the hum of machinery and the occasional screech of tires from nearby traffic can plunge him back into the moment of the accident, causing intense anxiety and difficulty focusing on his work. His colleagues have noticed how he seems more distant lately and often leaves meetings abruptly to step outside when certain sounds or smells remind him of the trauma. The cycle has tightened over time. John’s constant vigilance means that any trigger immediately brings back the memory, which in turn heightens his sense of threat. This heightened alertness then reinforces his belief in needing to be on guard all the time, creating a self-perpetuating loop. Despite his efforts to avoid triggers and manage his symptoms, John's quality of life has significantly declined. The constant intrusions into his daily routine have strained his relationships and impacted his work performance. What finally brought him to seek help was an overwhelming sense that he could no longer function effectively in his role as a financial analyst without addressing these fears. John is most afraid of losing control, both at home and at work. He hopes for relief from the intrusive memories and a return to a life where he can trust his surroundings again. With support, John believes he can regain some semblance of normalcy and find peace in knowing that his past does not have to dictate his present.
